_doc: Chronicle scheduler table for the finale, The Convergence. The rules are C1 in docs/story_wiring_v1.md, and the director that raises on_convergence is C6 there; the script is docs/chronicle_finale_v1.md. Beats are evaluated in file order on each raise; lineTokens maps each line token to its key in this file's lines. Keys that no token uses are director lines: the director reads them itself with ChronicleScheduler.Line.

Under your arm the Register murmurs that it has this on file: the full hall, the empty chair, the letter in the air. Another reading, the same hall. It turns to a clean page anyway.

Wenna Aldric stands along the wall with the graduating class, in the gap where you stood, in a borrowed robe buttoned to the throat. She has her spectacles folded in one hand. She does not look at the lectern, where she is also standing.

Wenna Aldric stands along the wall with the graduating class, in the gap where you stood. She came because the accession list left her no proper alternative, and she has told you so, in complete sentences. She has never left a sentence unfinished in her life. She does not mean to start tonight.
Only one Wenna Aldric is in the hall: the one at the lectern, with her mouth open on the next word. The other lost her seat to you, and is somewhere out in the running world, keeping a list.

Only one Wenna Aldric is in the hall: the one at the lectern, with her mouth open on the next word. The other is his now. The Severed Curriculum teaches everything her Academy taught, except how to stop.
Aurel Pendry stands behind his own chair, where the Aurel Pendry of that afternoon sits with a pen behind his ear. He has his shorthand open, and he is annotating the room.
Aurel Pendry stands behind his own chair, where your terms require him to stand. He corrected the terms twice before he signed them, both times in your favor. You still have not worked out why.
In the Reviser's chair the Aurel Pendry of that afternoon sits alone, a pen behind his ear. The other lost his seat to you, and his margins are empty.
In the Reviser's chair the Aurel Pendry of that afternoon sits alone. The other is his now, revising everything toward the Astrologer's preferred conclusion.

Hess is in her chair. It was empty at the naming; she left it before the wards broke. Tonight she came in by the side door and sat down in it without a word, and the crow on her shoulder is facing the east doors.
Hess is in her chair. Nobody can say what brought her. The land does not bargain, and neither, as far as anyone knows, does she.
Hess's chair is empty, as it was at the naming. Her seat was taken from her, and the land did not intervene.
Hess's chair is empty, as it was at the naming. The Severed Root does not come indoors.

Joren Kall stands behind his own chair, where the Joren Kall of that afternoon sits with the weather in his face. In here the argument in him has stopped. He looks like a man listening to one voice, and it is his.
Joren Kall stands behind his own chair. He came on terms, and he keeps his eyes on the east doors, where the weather will come in.
In the Vessel's chair the Joren Kall of that afternoon sits alone with the weather in his face. The other lost his seat to you, and the Covenant answers to the guild.
In the Vessel's chair the Joren Kall of that afternoon sits alone. The other is out in the Scoured, where one side of the argument won.

Cael Morn stands behind their own chair, every layer of them turned toward the east doors. They have not sat down. They have not said they are not finished, either, which you have learned is a layer of its own.
Cael Morn stands behind their own chair. The paper they put in your pocket is still there. They have not asked for it back.
In the Namer's chair the Cael Morn of that afternoon sits alone. The other lost their seat to you, layer by layer.
In the Namer's chair the Cael Morn of that afternoon sits alone. The other is with the Unwritten now, unmaking what they used to build.

Ondria Vell stands behind her own chair with a bottle she cannot open in here and has brought anyway. Now and then she looks along the line of the class to the third from the end, and then at the man in the back row, half risen from his seat.
Ondria Vell stands behind her own chair. She came on your terms. She has added them to the tab.
In the Conductor's chair the Ondria Vell of that afternoon sits alone. The other lost her seat to you, and nobody is pouring.
In the Conductor's chair the Ondria Vell of that afternoon sits alone. The other has closed the bar. The Silent Table serves no one.

Bram Korro stands behind his own chair with both hands in his pockets, because it is the only way he can keep them there. His notebook is open on the seat beside the Bram Korro of that afternoon, and he is writing down everything that has not happened yet.
Bram Korro stands behind his own chair, on terms he read twice and signed once. He has marked seventeen places where tonight could go wrong. He considers that optimistic.
In the Engineer's chair the Bram Korro of that afternoon sits alone, his hands folded so they will stay still. The other lost his workshop to you.
In the Engineer's chair the Bram Korro of that afternoon sits alone. The other builds without safety constraints now, in the Unshackled Forge.

When the last of them has spoken the hall is very quiet. Every answer in it is the same answer, each in its own words.
When the last of them has spoken, more than half the hall has given one answer, and the rest have not. The Register writes every word in the hand that said it, and does not count.
When the last of them has spoken, no answer has more than half the hall. The Register writes them all down and leaves the last line for your hand.
There is nobody to ask. The Register writes the question down anyway, in your hand, and leaves the answer to you.
You have reported to her three times. The nod is so nearly finished that the whole hall seems to lean toward it.
You have reported to her twice. The nod has come a long way since that morning. It has a little way still to go.
You reported to her once, after the first piece came home. The nod has moved since then. You are almost sure of it.
You have never reported to her. You meant to. The nod has waited for you anyway, exactly where it was.

The spell moves. After a year an arm's length from the place where you stood, it finishes its flight down the line it was drafted on, past that place, toward the lectern. Under your arm the Register falls open at Aurel Pendry's annotations, copied in his hand, and the spell, as if it had been reading over your shoulder, goes where the margin says. It misses. It passes the lectern by a hand's breadth and goes out against the stone behind the dais, and leaves a mark there no wider than a pen stroke. 'Received,' says the Register.

The spell moves. After a year an arm's length from the place where you stood, it finishes its flight down the line it was drafted on, past that place, toward the lectern, and strikes the letter of ink standing in the air above it. The letter shudders, and holds. It was never addressed to you. It was addressed to the next word, and the next word has not been said.
Far below, at the ring of stones under the fallen seat, the land takes hold. Out in the rain one of the Keepers stops, and cannot start again. At the end, the land will hold. It has begun early.

At the gatehouse the seventh layer fired, once, when it mattered. The second wave is still standing out in the rain on the far side of the arch, not one of them able to say why they cannot come in. Cael Morn has not moved from where they stood all night. 'Now,' they say, 'you may thank me.'
Every piece is home. Six refusals lie warm in the glass, waiting to be set back the way they were set the first time.
None of the pieces is home. The glass has nothing to give back but its own cold shards, and the breach knows it.
Not every piece is home. Where the missing ones should be the glass is dark, and the breach is wider there, and it will take longer to close.

You put both hands on the glass where {traitor_short}'s palm broke it, and begin anyway. The Fast has a word for what you are doing, and the word is refusal. With nothing to give back, you refuse on the world's behalf with your own hands, and hold the breach while the glass remembers how to close. Every round of it, something comes up through the breach to stop you.

You put both hands on the glass where {traitor_short}'s palm broke it, and begin. The Fast has a word for what you are doing, and the word is refusal. You give the glass back what it held, one piece at a time, and refuse on the world's behalf what each piece's maker refused. Each time, something comes up through the breach to stop you.

On the dais Hess sits in her chair and watches him come the way she has watched eight endings: without moving. He looks at her a moment. 'You left,' he says. 'I came back,' says Hess. That is all either of them says.

He has seen you before, in another reading, and you can tell from his face that he does not remember it. He looks at you the way you would look at a word in a language you never learned: closely, courteously, with no idea at all what it says. 'I have stood in this room before,' he says. 'I remember the ceiling. I do not remember you.' He frowns, very slightly. 'I find I cannot keep you.'
It is the first time he has seen you, and you can tell. He looks at you the way you would look at a word in a language you never learned: closely, courteously, with no idea at all what it says.
'I spoke to you once,' he says. 'In my reading room, to a place by the table where the passage bent. I did not know whether anyone was there.' He considers you. 'You were.'
'You refused my ending,' he says, mildly, as if remarking on the weather. 'As read. It is the only answer of yours I have ever read, and I read it off a messenger's face.'
'You accepted my ending,' he says. 'I sent it back. I could not read it, and I do not sign what I cannot read.' For a moment he looks almost rueful. 'I have wondered since what you meant by it.'

He looks past you at the glass, where the pieces are back in their places and the breach between them is closing. 'You mean to put it back,' he says. 'I have read that passage. It ends in a cold room.' He takes off his coat and folds it over the back of his empty chair. 'Very well. We will see who is standing in the room at the end of it.'

He looks at your hand, and at what is on it from the other side of the breach, and for the first time all night he seems unsettled. 'You went through,' he says. 'You mean to keep it.' A pause. 'Then you agree with me. You only disagree about whose hand.'

He looks at the clean page under your arm, where a hand that is not a hand has been writing, and reads it, or tries to. 'I cannot read that,' he says, very quietly. It is, you suspect, the first sentence he has spoken in years without knowing how it ends.

The titan goes out of him like weather leaving a field, and he is a man again, on one knee on the examination floor in front of the lectern, in the place where you stood that afternoon. 'You have put it back,' he says. He sounds tired, and not at all surprised. 'I hope you are right. I have read the room at the end of this passage. There is a lamp in it, and no one to hand it to.' He looks up at the glass, at the light in it. 'Perhaps you will be the one who proves me wrong. I would like that. I do not expect it.'

The breach goes out of him the way it came in, through the hands, and he is a man again, on one knee on the examination floor, in the place where you stood that afternoon. He looks at your hand for a long time. 'Then I was right,' he says, and he does not sound pleased. 'You agree with me. You only wanted it in your own hand.' He gets up, carefully. 'Be careful with it. Reading it and holding it are not the same. I have done the one. You are about to learn the other.'

He sits back on his heels on the examination floor, in the place where you stood that afternoon, and looks at the clean page under your arm, where the other hand is still writing. 'Half,' he says. 'You are telling me half of it was true.' He almost smiles. 'I did not read that. I did not read anything at all in here.' He listens a moment to the quiet. 'It is very restful, not knowing. I can see why you like it.'

In the glass the six lights that pulled apart at Commencement lean together again, until there is no gap between them a hand could go through. Every piece is in its place. The Seal is whole for the first time since the afternoon it broke.
No light comes back into the glass. It closes dark, all six places of it, and something will have to hold every one of them. Something always does.

In the glass the lights that came home lean together, until there is no gap between them a hand could go through. Where pieces are missing the glass is dark, and something will have to hold those places. Something always does.
Below the fallen seat, at the ring of stones, the crows have come down onto every stone. At the end, the land held.
In the morning, if the Second has mornings, someone counts who is still standing, and reads the count to you through the glass.
In the morning, if the Second has mornings, you count who is still standing.
They count again for you, out loud, at the glass. It comes out the same. You are glad.
You count them again. It comes out the same. You are glad.

The guild's honored dead were here too. You felt them when the glass took the pieces: a pressure at your back, the way a crowd presses forward when it wants to see. Their names are in the Register. They held the Seal while it set.
The guild's honored dead were in the breach with you. You saw them on the far side, at the edges of the dark, keeping pace. They did not follow you back. They did not seem to want to.
The guild's honored dead stood between you and the thing that was reading you, the way the dead stand between the living and the dark. It read them first. It was gentler after that.

Nobody steps up. Nobody in the hall has finished becoming who they would need to be for this, and you will not ask anyone who has not. So it is you. You lay both hands on the glass where {traitor_short}'s palm broke it, and the light comes up through your fingers, and you understand what it will cost: the rest of this reading. You will stay in the glass until the reading closes. Behind you someone says your name. It is the first time anyone has said it tonight.
